Microbiome correlation released R
SECOM (sparse estimation of correlations among microbiomes) estimates correlations between pairs of taxa, within one ecosystem or across ecosystems. secom_linear estimates sparse Pearson or Spearman correlations after bias correction. secom_dist estimates distance correlation, which also detects nonlinear relationships.

title: SECOM
text:
Extended tutorial
The R tutorial applies SECOM to the HITChip Atlas data set of intestinal microbiota profiles from Western adults, distributed with the microbiome package as atlas1006. The analysis estimates the correlation between each pair of taxa, aggregated at the Family rank of the data set.
Select a platform.

RPythonWeb tool



Model
Let \(o_{ij}\) denote the observed abundance and \(a_{ij}\) the unobserved absolute abundance of taxon \(i\) in sample \(j\). SECOM assumes
\[
\log o_{ij} = \log c_i + \log s_j + \log a_{ij},
\]
where \(c_i\) is the taxon-specific sequencing efficiency and \(s_j\) is the sample-specific sampling fraction. The term \(\log s_j\) is shared by all taxa in sample \(j\) and therefore induces correlation between observed abundances that is absent from the absolute abundances. SECOM estimates this sample-specific bias, subtracts it, and computes correlations from the bias-corrected log abundances.
Two estimators are available.








Function
Measure
Detects




secom_linear
Pearson or Spearman correlation
Linear or monotone relationships


secom_dist
Distance correlation
Linear and nonlinear relationships





Data

library(ANCOMBC)
library(tidyverse)

data(atlas1006, package = "microbiome")

# Baseline samples only, so that each subject contributes one sample.
pseq <- phyloseq::subset_samples(atlas1006, time == 0)
meta <- data.frame(phyloseq::sample_data(pseq))

# BMI in three ordered groups, with lean as the reference level.
meta$bmi <- fct_collapse(meta$bmi_group,
                         obese = c("obese", "severeobese", "morbidobese"))
meta$bmi <- factor(meta$bmi, levels = c("lean", "overweight", "obese"))

# Geographic region, with Central Europe as the reference level.
meta$region <- fct_collapse(meta$nationality,
                            CE = "CentralEurope", NE = c("Scandinavia", "UKIE"),
                            SE = "SouthEurope", EE = "EasternEurope", US = "US")

phyloseq::sample_data(pseq) <- meta
tse <- mia::convertFromPhyloseq(pseq)
tse

Linear correlation

set.seed(123)
res_linear <- secom_linear(data = list(tse), assay_name = "counts",
                           tax_level = "Family", pseudo = 0,
                           prv_cut = 0.5, lib_cut = 1000, corr_cut = 0.5,
                           wins_quant = c(0.05, 0.95), method = "pearson",
                           soft = FALSE, thresh_len = 20, n_cv = 10,
                           thresh_hard = 0.3, max_p = 0.005, n_cl = 2)








Argument
Role




data
A list of data objects, one per ecosystem. One element gives correlations within one ecosystem.


prv_cut
Taxa present in a smaller proportion of samples are excluded.


corr_cut
A taxon whose correlation with the estimated sample-specific bias exceeds this value is flagged, and its pairwise correlations are set to 0.


wins_quant
Quantiles at which extreme abundances are winsorized.


soft, thresh_len, n_cv
Thresholding operator, number of candidate thresholds, and number of cross-validation folds for the thresholded estimate.


thresh_hard
Correlations with absolute value at or below this value are set to 0.


max_p
Correlations with a p-value above this value are set to 0 in the filtered estimate.



The result contains three estimates of the correlation matrix.







Element
Content




corr
Sample correlation matrix of the bias-corrected abundances


corr_th
Sparse matrix obtained by thresholding, with the threshold chosen by cross-validation


corr_fl
Sparse matrix obtained by p-value filtering at max_p



A function for drawing a correlation matrix is defined once and used for each estimate.

plot_corr <- function(mat, limits = c(-1, 1), label = "Correlation") {
  as.data.frame(as.table(mat)) |>
    setNames(c("taxon1", "taxon2", "value")) |>
    mutate(taxon2 = fct_rev(taxon2)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = taxon1, y = taxon2, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(value == 0, "", sprintf("%.2f", value))),
              size = 2.6) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3f9ae0", mid = "white", high = "#f2775f",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = limits, name = label) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}


plot_corr(res_linear$corr_fl)

Distance correlation
Distance correlation takes values in \([0, 1]\) and equals 0 only under independence. The p-values are obtained from R permutation replicates.

set.seed(123)
res_dist <- secom_dist(data = list(tse), assay_name = "counts",
                       tax_level = "Family", pseudo = 0,
                       prv_cut = 0.5, lib_cut = 1000, corr_cut = 0.5,
                       wins_quant = c(0.05, 0.95), R = 1000,
                       thresh_hard = 0.3, max_p = 0.005, n_cl = 2)


plot_corr(res_dist$dcorr_fl, limits = c(0, 1), label = "Distance\ncorrelation")







Figure 3: Distance correlation after p-value filtering (dcorr_fl). Empty cells are correlations set to 0.







Comparison of the two estimators
A pair of taxa with a nonzero filtered distance correlation and a zero filtered Pearson correlation is a candidate for a nonlinear relationship.

upper <- upper.tri(res_linear$corr_fl)
taxa  <- rownames(res_linear$corr_fl)

pairs <- tibble(
  taxon1   = taxa[row(res_linear$corr_fl)[upper]],
  taxon2   = taxa[col(res_linear$corr_fl)[upper]],
  pearson  = res_linear$corr_fl[upper],
  distance = res_dist$dcorr_fl[upper]
)

c(pairs               = nrow(pairs),
  pearson_nonzero     = sum(pairs$pearson != 0),
  distance_nonzero    = sum(pairs$distance != 0),
  distance_only       = sum(pairs$distance != 0 & pairs$pearson == 0))

title: TriGer
text:
Multi-omics integration released R Python MATLAB
TriGer (triple-graph model) detects modules of features from two omics layers \(X\) and \(Y\). It uses three association matrices: the cross-omics matrix between \(X\) and \(Y\), and the within-omics correlation matrices of \(X\) and of \(Y\). Dense blocks are first extracted from the cross-omics matrix by greedy peeling, and large blocks are then refined with the within-omics matrices. Each module is therefore densely associated across the two layers and coherent within each layer. The parameter lambda1 is the size penalty of the cross-omics step, and lambda2 and lambda3 are the within-omics penalties for \(X\) and \(Y\); larger values give smaller, denser modules.

title: TriGer
text:
Extended tutorial
The R tutorial detects modules of gut bacterial genera and stool metabolites in the PRISM and validation cohorts of Franzosa et al. (2019), which include patients with Crohn’s disease (CD), patients with ulcerative colitis (UC), and controls. The data are the processed metagenomic and metabolomic tables of the curated microbiome–metabolome collection of Muller et al. (2022). The modules are detected from all samples, and the strength of each module is then compared between the diagnosis groups.
Select a platform.

RPythonMATLAB



Model
Let \(\mathbf{X}\) denote the \(n \times m\) matrix of the first omics layer and \(\mathbf{Y}\) the \(n \times q\) matrix of the second, with the same \(n\) samples in rows. Let \(\mathbf{Z} = [\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{Y}]\) denote their combination, with \(m + q\) columns. Let \(r_{ab}\) denote the correlation of columns \(a\) and \(b\) of \(\mathbf{Z}\), and let \(p_{ab}\) denote the p-value of the test of zero correlation. TriGer uses the \((m + q) \times (m + q)\) matrices
\[
\mathbf{R} = (r_{ab})
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{P} = (-\log_{10} p_{ab}).
\]
The cross-omics block of \(\mathbf{P}\), with rows \(1, \ldots, m\) and columns \(m + 1, \ldots, m + q\), defines a weighted bipartite graph between the features of \(X\) and \(Y\). The within-omics blocks of \(\mathbf{R}\) define one weighted graph for each layer; together with the bipartite graph they form the triple graph. In the first step, TriGer extracts dense blocks of the bipartite graph by greedy peeling, with size penalty \(\lambda_1\). In the second and third steps, the \(X\) side and the \(Y\) side of each block that exceeds a maximum size are divided into dense communities of the corresponding within-omics graph, with size penalties \(\lambda_2\) and \(\lambda_3\). A module is a resulting set of \(X\) features and \(Y\) features.


Data
The \(X\) layer consists of the bacterial genera with a prevalence of at least 50% and a mean relative abundance of at least 0.2%, on the centered log-ratio (CLR) scale. The \(Y\) layer consists of the named metabolites with at most 30% zeros, on the log scale; features with the same HMDB identifier, or without one and with names that differ only by a trailing asterisk, are treated as one compound. In both layers, zeros are replaced by half of the smallest positive value of the feature.

library(TriGer)
library(tidyverse)

url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/borenstein-lab/",
              "microbiome-metabolome-curated-data/main/data/processed_data/",
              "FRANZOSA_IBD_2019/")

meta <- read.delim(paste0(url, "metadata.tsv"), check.names = FALSE)
fmap <- read.delim(paste0(url, "mtb.map.tsv"), check.names = FALSE)
mtb  <- as.matrix(read.delim(paste0(url, "mtb.tsv"), check.names = FALSE, row.names = 1))
gen  <- as.matrix(read.delim(paste0(url, "genera.tsv"), check.names = FALSE, row.names = 1))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(mtb), meta$Sample), identical(rownames(gen), meta$Sample))

half_min <- function(v) { v[v == 0] <- min(v[v > 0]) / 2; v }

# X: genera, CLR over the retained genera.
gen <- gen[, colMeans(gen > 0) >= 0.5 & colMeans(gen) >= 0.002]
colnames(gen) <- sub(".*;g__", "", colnames(gen))
log_gen <- log(apply(gen, 2, half_min))
x <- log_gen - rowMeans(log_gen)

# Y: named metabolites, one feature per compound, log scale.
named <- fmap |>
  filter(!is.na(Compound.Name), Compound %in% colnames(mtb)) |>
  mutate(name = str_remove(Compound.Name, "[*]+$"),
         key  = coalesce(HMDB, name),
         zero = colMeans(mtb[, Compound] == 0)) |>
  arrange(key, zero) |>
  distinct(key, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  filter(zero <= 0.3)
y <- log(apply(mtb[, named$Compound], 2, half_min))
colnames(y) <- named$name

c(samples = nrow(x), genera = ncol(x), metabolites = ncol(y))

#>     samples      genera metabolites 
#>         220          73         291




Analysis

res <- triger(x, y, method = "spearman",
              lambda1 = 1.5, lambda2 = 1.8, lambda3 = 1.8,
              X_size = c(3, 25), Y_size = c(5, 50))
length(res$modules)

title: ANCOM-BC
text:
Extended tutorial
The R tutorial applies ANCOM-BC to the HITChip Atlas data set of intestinal microbiota profiles from Western adults, distributed with the microbiome package as atlas1006. The analysis tests whether the abundance of each taxon, aggregated at the Family rank of the data set, differs between body mass index (BMI) groups, adjusted for age and geographic region.
Select a platform.

RPythonQIIME 2Web tool



Model
Let \(o_{ij}\) denote the observed abundance of taxon \(i\) in sample \(j\), and let \(\mathbf{x}_j\) denote the covariate vector of sample \(j\), including an intercept. ANCOM-BC assumes
\[
\log o_{ij} = d_j + \mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}_i + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where \(d_j\) is the log sampling fraction of sample \(j\) and \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is a mean-zero error. The sampling fraction is not observed and differs between samples, which biases an unadjusted comparison of observed abundances. ANCOM-BC estimates \(d_j\), and for coefficient \(k\) of taxon \(i\) tests
\[
H_0: \beta_{ik} = 0 \quad \text{with} \quad W_{ik} = \hat{\beta}_{ik} / \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat{\beta}_{ik}).
\]
The coefficient \(\beta_{ik}\) is a log fold change in absolute abundance on the natural-log scale.


Data

library(ANCOMBC)
library(tidyverse)

data(atlas1006, package = "microbiome")

# Baseline samples only, so that each subject contributes one sample.
pseq <- phyloseq::subset_samples(atlas1006, time == 0)
meta <- data.frame(phyloseq::sample_data(pseq))

# BMI in three groups, with lean as the reference level.
meta$bmi <- fct_collapse(meta$bmi_group,
                         obese = c("obese", "severeobese", "morbidobese"))
meta$bmi <- factor(meta$bmi, levels = c("lean", "overweight", "obese"))

# Geographic region, with Central Europe as the reference level.
meta$region <- fct_collapse(meta$nationality,
                            CE = "CentralEurope", NE = c("Scandinavia", "UKIE"),
                            SE = "SouthEurope", EE = "EasternEurope", US = "US")

phyloseq::sample_data(pseq) <- meta
tse <- mia::convertFromPhyloseq(pseq)

title: MetVAE
text:
Metabolomics correlation released R Python GNPS
MetVAE constructs a correlation network from untargeted metabolomics data. Zeros in the abundance table are treated as values below the detection limit and imputed by a variational autoencoder. The effects of the specified sample covariates are removed, and a sparse correlation matrix between metabolite features is estimated. Pairs are retained either by Fisher z-tests with multiple-testing correction (sparse_by_p) or by the sparse estimation of correlation (SEC) estimator with a penalty selected by cross-validation (sparse_by_sec).

title: MetVAE
text:
Extended tutorial
The R tutorial estimates a metabolite correlation network from the stool metabolomes of the PRISM and validation cohorts of Franzosa et al. (2019), which include patients with Crohn’s disease (CD), patients with ulcerative colitis (UC), and controls. The data are the processed tables of the curated microbiome–metabolome collection of Muller et al. (2022). The network is adjusted for diagnosis, age, and cohort, so that it describes the co-variation of metabolites within these strata.
Select a platform.

RPythonGNPS



Model
Let \(y_{ij}\) denote the abundance of metabolite \(j\) in sample \(i\), for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) and \(j = 1, \ldots, p\), and let \(z_{ij}\) denote its value on the centered log-ratio (CLR) scale. Let \(\mathbf{x}_i\) denote the covariate vector of sample \(i\). MetVAE assumes the left-censored normal model
\[
z_{ij} = \mu_j + \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma}_j + \sigma_j \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, 1),
\]
in which a zero is recorded when the abundance falls below the detection limit. The parameters \(\mu_j\), \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_j\), and \(\sigma_j\) are estimated under censoring, and the covariate effects are removed. A variational autoencoder trained on the adjusted data imputes the censored values \(M\) times. For imputation \(s\), let \(\tilde{z}^{(s)}_{ij}\) denote the completed adjusted data. The correlation of metabolites \(j\) and \(k\) is estimated from the variance of their log ratio,
\[
\hat{r}^{(s)}_{jk} = \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\big(\tilde{z}^{(s)}_{\cdot j}\big) + \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\big(\tilde{z}^{(s)}_{\cdot k}\big) - \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\big(\tilde{z}^{(s)}_{\cdot j} - \tilde{z}^{(s)}_{\cdot k}\big)}{2 \, \widehat{\mathrm{SD}}\big(\tilde{z}^{(s)}_{\cdot j}\big) \, \widehat{\mathrm{SD}}\big(\tilde{z}^{(s)}_{\cdot k}\big)},
\]
and the estimate \(\hat{r}_{jk}\) is the mean of \(\hat{r}^{(s)}_{jk}\) over the \(M\) imputations, after entries with \(|\hat{r}^{(s)}_{jk}|\) below a threshold are set to zero.
Two procedures produce a sparse network. The first tests \(H_0: r_{jk} = 0\) with
\[
T_{jk} = \operatorname{atanh}(\hat{r}_{jk}) \sqrt{n - 3}
\]
and retains the pairs whose adjusted p-value is below a cutoff. The second, SEC (Cui, Leng and Sun, 2016), solves
\[
\hat{\mathbf{R}} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{R}} \; \tfrac{1}{2} \lVert \mathbf{R} - \hat{\mathbf{R}}_0 \rVert_F^2 + \rho \sum_{j \ne k} \frac{|R_{jk}|}{|\hat{r}_{jk}|}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{R}) \ge \epsilon,
\]
where \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}_0\) is the matrix of the estimates \(\hat{r}_{jk}\), and the penalty \(\rho\) is selected by cross-validation.


Data
The metabolomics table has one row per sample and one column per LC-MS feature. The tutorial retains the features with a compound name. Features with the same HMDB identifier, or without one and with names that differ only by a trailing asterisk, are treated as one compound, and for each compound the feature with the smallest proportion of zeros is retained.

library(MetVAE)
library(tidyverse)
library(igraph)

url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/borenstein-lab/",
              "microbiome-metabolome-curated-data/main/data/processed_data/",
              "FRANZOSA_IBD_2019/")

meta <- read.delim(paste0(url, "metadata.tsv"), check.names = FALSE)
fmap <- read.delim(paste0(url, "mtb.map.tsv"), check.names = FALSE)
mtb  <- read.delim(paste0(url, "mtb.tsv"), check.names = FALSE, row.names = 1)
mtb  <- as.matrix(mtb)

# Features with a compound name; one feature per compound.
named <- fmap |>
  filter(!is.na(Compound.Name), Compound %in% colnames(mtb)) |>
  mutate(name = str_remove(Compound.Name, "[*]+$"),
         key  = coalesce(HMDB, name),
         zero = colMeans(mtb[, Compound] == 0),
         med  = apply(mtb[, Compound], 2, median)) |>
  arrange(key, zero, desc(med)) |>
  distinct(key, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE)

Correlation estimate

Sparse networks

res_p   <- sparse_by_p(fit, p_adj_method = "fdr_bh", cutoff = 0.05)
res_sec <- sparse_by_sec(fit, c_grid = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8),
                         refine = FALSE, seed = 1L)

n_edges <- function(m) (Matrix::nnzero(m) - nrow(m)) / 2
c(fdr = n_edges(res_p$sparse_estimate), sec = n_edges(res_sec$sparse_estimate))

#>   fdr   sec

res_sec$scores_by_rho |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rho, y = score)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey30") +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = res_sec$best_rho, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = expression(rho ~ "(log scale)"), y = "Validation error") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







Figure 3: Cross-validation error of SEC by penalty. The dashed line marks the selected penalty.





The grid of the penalty is \(\rho = c \sqrt{\log p / n}\) for the listed values of \(c\). The validation error decreases as \(\rho\) decreases over the whole grid, and cross-validation selects the smallest value, \(\rho =\) 0.00803. In these data the penalty therefore shrinks the estimate little, and the zeros of the SEC estimate arise mainly from the thresholds of get_corr() (0.2) and sparse_by_sec() (0.1).

title: ANCOM-BC2
text:
Extended tutorial
The R tutorial applies ANCOM-BC2 to the HITChip Atlas data set of intestinal microbiota profiles from Western adults, distributed with the microbiome package as atlas1006. The analysis compares the abundance of each taxon, aggregated at the Family rank of the data set, across three body mass index (BMI) groups (lean, overweight, obese), adjusted for age and geographic region.
Select a platform.

RPythonQIIME 2Web tool



Model and hypotheses
Let \(o_{ij}\) denote the observed abundance of taxon \(i\) in sample \(j\), and let \(\mathbf{x}_j\) denote the covariate vector of sample \(j\), including an intercept. ANCOM-BC2 assumes
\[
\log o_{ij} = d_j + \mathbf{x}_j^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}_i + \varepsilon_{ij},
\]
where \(d_j\) is the log sampling fraction of sample \(j\) and \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is a mean-zero error. For repeated measures, random effects are added to the linear predictor through rand_formula.
Let \(\beta_{i,\mathrm{ow}}\) and \(\beta_{i,\mathrm{ob}}\) denote the coefficients of taxon \(i\) for the overweight and obese groups, with lean as the reference. The analysis tests four families of hypotheses.








Test
Null hypothesis
Alternative




Primary
\(\beta_{ik} = 0\) for one coefficient \(k\)
\(\beta_{ik} \neq 0\)


Global
\(\beta_{i,\mathrm{ow}} = \beta_{i,\mathrm{ob}} = 0\)
at least one is nonzero


Pairwise directional
equal abundance in a pair of groups, for every pair
a difference with its direction


Dunnett type
equal abundance in a group and the reference, for every non-reference group
a difference with its direction


Trend
\(\beta_{i,\mathrm{ow}} = \beta_{i,\mathrm{ob}} = 0\)
a monotone pattern across the ordered groups



The pairwise and Dunnett-type tests control the mixed directional false discovery rate, which accounts for both the multiple comparisons within a taxon and the multiplicity across taxa.


Data

library(ANCOMBC)
library(tidyverse)

data(atlas1006, package = "microbiome")

# Baseline samples only, so that each subject contributes one sample.
pseq <- phyloseq::subset_samples(atlas1006, time == 0)
meta <- data.frame(phyloseq::sample_data(pseq))

# BMI in three ordered groups, with lean as the reference level.
meta$bmi <- fct_collapse(meta$bmi_group,
                         obese = c("obese", "severeobese", "morbidobese"))
meta$bmi <- factor(meta$bmi, levels = c("lean", "overweight", "obese"))

# Geographic region, with Central Europe as the reference level.
meta$region <- fct_collapse(meta$nationality,
                            CE = "CentralEurope", NE = c("Scandinavia", "UKIE"),
                            SE = "SouthEurope", EE = "EasternEurope", US = "US")

phyloseq::sample_data(pseq) <- meta
tse <- mia::convertFromPhyloseq(pseq)
tse

Analysis
The trend test requires the monotone patterns as inequality constraints \(A\boldsymbol{\theta} \ge 0\) on \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\beta_{i,\mathrm{ow}}, \beta_{i,\mathrm{ob}})^\top\). The pattern \(0 \le \beta_{i,\mathrm{ow}} \le \beta_{i,\mathrm{ob}}\) (increasing) and the pattern \(0 \ge \beta_{i,\mathrm{ow}} \ge \beta_{i,\mathrm{ob}}\) (decreasing) are specified as two contrast matrices.

increasing <- matrix(c( 1, 0,
                       -1, 1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
decreasing <- matrix(c(-1,  0,
                        1, -1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)


set.seed(123)
out <- ancombc2(data = tse, assay_name = "counts", tax_level = "Family",
                fix_formula = "age + region + bmi", rand_formula = NULL,
                p_adj_method = "holm", pseudo_sens = TRUE,
                prv_cut = 0.10, lib_cut = 1000, s0_perc = 0.05,
                group = "bmi", struc_zero = TRUE, neg_lb = TRUE,
                alpha = 0.05, n_cl = 2, verbose = FALSE,
                global = TRUE, pairwise = TRUE, dunnet = TRUE, trend = TRUE,
                iter_control = list(tol = 1e-2, max_iter = 20, verbose = FALSE),
                em_control = list(tol = 1e-5, max_iter = 100),
                lme_control = lme4::lmerControl(),
                mdfdr_control = list(fwer_ctrl_method = "holm", B = 100),
                trend_control = list(contrast = list(increasing, decreasing),
                                     node = list(2, 2),
                                     solver = "ECOS", B = 100))








Argument
Role




fix_formula, rand_formula
Fixed and random effects of the log-linear model.


group
Grouping variable for structural zero detection and for the global, pairwise, Dunnett-type, and trend tests.


pseudo_sens
Sensitivity analysis of each result to the addition of pseudo-counts to zeros.


s0_perc
Percentile of the standard errors added to the denominator of the test statistic, which limits significance caused by very small standard errors.


global, pairwise, dunnet, trend
Multigroup tests to perform.


mdfdr_control
Procedure and number of bootstrap samples B for the mixed directional false discovery rate.


trend_control
Contrast matrices, position of the nodal parameter, and number of bootstrap samples B for the trend test.

The element res is a data frame with one row per taxon. For each model coefficient it contains the following columns.







Column prefix
Content

p-value and adjusted p-value


diff_
TRUE if the adjusted p-value is below alpha


passed_ss_
TRUE if the result does not change with the pseudo-count added to zeros


diff_robust_
TRUE if both diff_ and passed_ss_ are TRUE
